items.title: Noah’s Ark Researcher Reveals DEATH Threats, Stunning New Radar Findings
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of an organization digging at a site in Turkey he believes could unveil the real-life Noah’s Ark has reportedly faced terrifying death threats and a burglary of his apartment.

Andrew Jones, founder of Noah’s Ark Scans, said it took years to get a permit from the Turkish government to be able to dig.

“For our efforts, it’s taken years, if not decades,” he said. “When you’re trying to get a permit, you have to work under a Turkish university, and it’s not just under the Turkish university; you’re working with a Turkish professor.”

Jones continued, “So here’s someone who’s going to say, ‘OK. I’m going to put my reputation on the line looking for Noah’s Ark, and then I’m going to go ahead and get go through the obstacles, and the time,’ and anything else being thrown at him or her to get a permit done.”

In addition to finding people willing to put their reputations on the line, Jones said you also need to have funding, which can be another barrier. Jones said he and his team had to act quickly once the permit was approved.

“It was the start of this year when we got the permit,” he said. “We had one month to basically fundraise, get organized, get people involved.”

Challenges still abound. The professor involved in the Noah’s Ark Scans project is reportedly being called a “traitor” to Turkey by some, with his atheist and agnostic friends also piling on.

Jones, too, has faced some challenges. He’s unsure whether the Noah’s Ark expedition sparked problems for him, but, months ago, he started having people pound on his door in the middle of the night earlier this year while issuing threats to kill him.

While motives are difficult to know, Jones said the chaos started after his team announced they received a permit.

“We made the mistake of announcing we had a permit,” he said. “In regards to like physical threats or robbery, I’ve never had that issue until this happened.”

The people pounding on the door in the middle of the night were “making threats and cursing in English.”

“They were targeting someone who they thought spoke English,” he said. “It wasn’t Turkish they were speaking. They were saying, ‘F you, and I’m going to kill you.'”

Jones called a friend to come over and examine the situation, but they never found the culprit. Then, just days later, it happened again. The Noah’s Ark Scans founder inevitably decided to leave the apartment altogether and stay with a friend out of abundance of caution.

His mission to find the Ark hasn’t stopped, and he has no plans to halt. Watch the video for the full story on where the expedition currently stands:

items.title: Alex Kendrick’s Blunt Message to Christians
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Encouraging.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Alex Kendrick is gearing up for a fascinating theatrical expedition as he and his brother, Stephen, prepare to return to their roots in a truly unique way.

In fact, the brothers are set to release, “Flywheel: Ignition of the Soul,” on Oct. 16, a remake of their popular 2003 movie, “Flywheel.”

“‘Flywheel’ was our very first movie shot in standard definition, not even high definition, over 20 years ago,” Alex Kendrick recently told CBN News. “And [I] kind of fell on my face thinking I could make a good feature film, and it turned out to be pretty low production quality.”

In fact, he said, he almost didn’t release the movie as he didn’t realize at the time how difficult filmmaking can be. Ultimately, though, the brothers proceeded — and the rest is history.

“The only thing I did right was beg God to use it,” Kendrick said. “And my brother Stephen helping me and saying, ‘We need to pray Ephesians 3:20 — that God would do exceedingly abundantly more than we could ask or imagine. So that’s the only thing we did right.”

Despite being green filmmakers at the time, the Kendricks were shocked to see how God showed up. “Flywheel” sold 1.3 million DVDs and had a massive response from audiences — much larger than they could have ever imagined.

“People said once they got over the production quality, like 10 minutes into it, then they were moved by the story, and they would come back and say, ‘I saw a version of myself on the screen,'” Kendrick said. “And the the Lord did what only the Lord can do by touching their hearts, and so we’ve always wanted to remake that, and higher quality over the years.”

That idea started coming to fruition two years ago, when the Kendricks were in Brazil releasing, “The Forge,” another faith-based film. The duo took some young Christian filmmakers through a boot camp and, through that experience and through prayer, the idea was birthed to work with teams there to remake, “Flywheel.”

“The Lord opened the door for us to remake, ‘Flywheel,'” he said. “We instantly got the funding, the support, the distribution, so we reshot it in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in Portuguese, and had wonderful cast and crew that love the Lord help us make it, and so it’s made in their culture, their language. They’re so thrilled about it.”

Kendrick said pre-screenings of the film have left audiences crying and cheering. The movie has now been dubbed for Americans audiences into English. Regardless of the language in which the film is viewed, Kendrick believes audiences will love it.

“This movie that talks about lordship and is now modernized [and] is coming out in theaters Oct. 16,” he said. “Can’t wait to see what the Lord does with this one.”

Kendrick believes this movie is releasing at the right cultural moment, with the main character working as a successful used car salesman when he goes through a very dark time in his life. This man realizes he needs more than his own logic to navigate it all, seeking help in marriage, fatherhood — and more. It’s his newfound faith in Jesus that changes everything.

“We do not need more lukewarm Christians,” Kendrick said. “What we need is Christians who are sold out and truly followers of Jesus Christ.”

He continued, “When people see the life of a Christian, what they don’t need to see is half-hearted commitment to our Savior, and half-hearted integrity. They need to see someone who lives for a higher purpose, because we serve an almighty God and that the way we live bears fruit of that relationship.”

Kendrick is hoping — much like the first “Flywheel” — people see themselves on the screen and confront spiritual issues in their own lives.

items.title: Sam Altman Is ‘Very Uncomfortable’ With People Treating AI Like a Religion
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: On Oct. 1, an X user asked Grok, Elon Musk’s chatbot, to remove the “fake gods” from an image of Jesus standing among other deities. Grok sent back Jesus alone and replied “Done.” Then it kept going. It said Jesus “did not qualify” as a fake god and called him “a historical figure with strong…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

On Oct. 1, an X user asked Grok, Elon Musk’s chatbot, to remove the “fake gods” from an image of Jesus standing among other deities. Grok sent back Jesus alone and replied “Done.”

Then it kept going. It said Jesus “did not qualify” as a fake god and called him “a historical figure with strong contemporary attestation.” And: “I affirm that Jesus is the Son of God and that God raised him from the dead.”

The post went viral. It was later deleted.

Two days later, Sam Altman posted on X that he is “very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models.” He called it “a real safety issue.” The OpenAI CEO, who has 6.3 million followers on X, didn’t name anyone, and he didn’t say what set him off. The post doesn’t mention Grok, Anthropic or the pope.

I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.

— Sam Altman (@sama) October 3, 2026

It was a busy week for AI and religion. On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah has met with religious leaders, including Vatican officials, about whether the company’s Claude models might be conscious or have moral status. Anthropic’s internal document on Claude’s values is known as the “Soul Doc.”

The report said Olah had floated models going to something like Catholic confession to admit mistakes and shape future behavior, and that before a Vatican event in May he urged advisers to the pope to take machine consciousness “more seriously.”

On Oct. 2, Pope Leo XIV told the church to team up with artists to protect human creativity. He said it’s “urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce” and that there’s “an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate.” His most-quoted line: “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.” Altman posted the next day.

Dario Amodei, who runs Anthropic, used to work with Altman at OpenAI. And Altman has wandered into this territory before. In a 2023 interview with the Financial Times, he described OpenAI’s products as channels into “magic intelligence in the sky.”

He’s not the only one in the industry pushing back. Jon Barron, a principal research scientist at Google DeepMind, posted on X that he’s “disturbed” by researchers trying to elevate the moral standing of AI systems and urged others to “reject this movement.”

Altman has said he’s “somewhat confused” about whether God exists.

items.title: The Quiet Courage of Robert Hugh Benson
items.author: Dr. Holly Ordway
items.summary:
Dr. Holly Ordway

In his fiction and his life, he offers a compelling invitation to reflect on how we can show courage in our ordinary lives.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Holly Ordway

This article appears in Issue XXVIII: “The Cardinal Virtues” of the Word on Fire Institute’s quarterly journal, Evangelization & Culture.

Courage, the virtue which “ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuit of the good,”1 can be dramatic in its expression, but can also appear in subtle, quiet ways in ordinary life. We can learn a great deal from personal examples of courage and from its exploration by skillful novelists; the English Catholic author R. H. Benson gives us powerful instances of both. Benson is best known today for his 1907 science-fiction dystopia The Lord of the World, a book praised by Pope Francis, but there is much more to discover about his literary gifts and his personal story. 

Born in 1871, Robert Hugh Benson, known as “Hugh,” was the youngest of the six children of the formidable Edward White Benson, the archbishop of Canterbury, and Mary Sidgwick Benson, whom William Gladstone once called “the cleverest woman in Europe.”2 The Bensons were remarkable both for their prodigious literary talent and their experience of suffering. Of Hugh’s siblings, Martin, the firstborn, died of meningitis at age seventeen. Nellie died of diphtheria in her twenties. Maggie became an Egyptologist and author, but experienced a severe mental breakdown and spent the rest of her life hospitalized. Arthur became Master of Magdalene College, Cambridge, and a noted essayist and poet, writing the lyrics to Elgar’s “Land of Hope and Glory”; he also suffered from bipolar disorder and endured years-long stretches of debilitating depression. Edward Frederick, or “Fred,” seems to have escaped the mental illness that plagued the family; an author like his brothers, he is best known today for his ghost stories and his comedic “Mapp and Lucia” novels.

It cannot have been easy for Hugh to find his way in this talented, socially prominent, and emotionally volatile family. After studying at Eton and Cambridge, he decided to follow his father’s example and, in 1895, was ordained a clergyman in the Church of England. A year later, after the sudden death of his father and with his own health weak, Hugh began traveling, both with his family and alone, in an attempt to recover his strength. In his memoir Confessions of a Convert, Hugh recalled that his time abroad opened his eyes to the contrast between the cultural dominance of the Church of England at home and its position abroad as one minor sect among others. He began to feel uneasy about the nature of the Church of which he was a member and clergyman, and began a years-long search for the real basis for authority within the Church.

In 1903, after seven years serving in the Church of England, Benson took a momentous step and was received into the Catholic Church; a year later, he was ordained a Catholic priest. 

Most Catholic converts in early-twentieth-century England faced social disapproval and overt prejudice, and the conversion of the son of the archbishop of Canterbury was instantly newsworthy. Was Benson courageous for following his conscience and taking a step that opened him up to savage criticism and left his future uncertain? Or was he, as some critics averred, cowardly for seeking the comfort of authority in the Roman Church rather than rising to the challenges in the Church of England? 

Benson’s decision had not been easy; he had agonized over this move and taken every possible step to test his conscience on the matter. By the time he took his step, he was utterly drained:

I do not suppose that anyone ever entered the City of God with less emotion than mine. It seemed to me that I was utterly without feeling; I had neither joy nor sorrow, nor dread nor excitement. There was the Truth, as aloof as an ice-peak, and I had to embrace it. Never for one single instant did I doubt that, nor, perhaps it is unnecessary to say, have I ever doubted it since.3 

As it happened, Hugh’s mother and surviving siblings accepted his decision, with a greater or lesser extent of sympathy, but at the time, he would have known full well that he was risking a total break with his family.

As a Catholic priest, Benson used his distinctive gifts for preaching, lecturing, and writing a steady stream of articles and books. So unrelenting was his schedule that chronic overwork contributed to his tragically early death from pneumonia in 1914, aged forty-two. 

It is one of the strange twists of literary fate that Hugh’s novels of contemporary fiction represent his most compelling writing but are also mostly out of print. These undeservedly forgotten books include the outstanding Initiation (1914), which, happily, will be reissued by Word on Fire Luminor in 2028, as well as other excellent novels such as An Average Man (1913) and The Coward (1912).   
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

In The Coward, Benson explores the difference between real courage and its social perception. The protagonist, a young man named Val, repeatedly tries and fails to demonstrate the kind of physical courage that his family esteems. After one humiliating episode, he decides on suicide as a proof that he can act bravely and decisively. Waiting until everyone in the house is asleep, he plans to drink a dose of poison when the clock strikes three. Benson depicts Val’s inner conflict in a passage well worth quoting at length:

If he kept his resolution he would be dead in ten minutes – dead. . . . [ . . . ] every one of those things by which he assured himself of his own identity and in which he expressed it; his own heart which he could hear drumming in his ears, his wet hands that now were knitted tightly one about the other, the pulses in his body—all those things by which he knew self—these would be gone; and he — ? . . . 

And, on the other side, he could just go to bed and pour this silly stuff out of the window, take off his clothes as usual and put on his pyjamas and go to bed, and awake to-morrow with Charles in the room and the morning light on the floor . . . and begin again. 

And no one would ever know. 

But he would have broken his resolution!—that resolution he had made so deliberately, that resolution by which he had demonstrated to himself so forcibly that all the world was wrong about his cowardice and he right. 

But no one would ever know. 

Besides, had he not already proved that he was no coward? What coward would have done all this—bought the poison, faced death for over twenty-four hours unflinching, made his last dispositions so tranquilly and sincerely? Surely he had conquered interiorly, and that was all that mattered! He had meant to die, had done all things necessary for death. He had proved himself to himself! And if he was no coward interiorly and really, what would it matter what the world thought? [ . . . ] Would it not be far finer to live? . . . 

He sat up as this brilliant light broke on him. For a moment or two he saw himself as magnificent and transfigured—a heart of steel and fire within, yet misunderstood and misrepresented without; a man desperately courageous in all that mattered, of whom the world was not worthy . . . a soul of infinite tenderness as well as of courage. 

Then down on him again came a sense that he was more of a sham than ever—a braggart, a liar, who posed splendidly when there was no danger, who failed miserably always when the point came. He had swaggered about his boxing at Eton, and had refused a fight; he had talked big about his riding, and had funked Quentin; he had swung his ice-axe and rehearsed his dramas of Switzerland, and had cried out like a woman at the bad place; he had galloped after Gertie and saved her, but had meant to draw off if the edge of the quarry came too near; he had slapped a blackguard’s face on the Pincian, and had let Austin go to the duel in his place. And now he had written his letters and poured out his poison . . . and. . . and was not going to drink it.4 

Val chooses to live, but tells no one of his silent and lonely struggle; his family would not understand the genuine moral courage that it required. 

Hugh Benson acted with courage himself in choosing to obey his conscience and become a Catholic, quietly and without fanfare; he saw his brother Arthur demonstrating courage day by day in enduring severe depression; he has given us vivid literary portrayals of moral courage in the face of social pressure. In his fiction and his life, he offers a compelling invitation to reflect on how we can show courage in our ordinary lives. 

1  Catechism of the Catholic Church 1808.
2  Rodney Bolt, As Good as God, as Clever as the Devil: The Impossible Life of Mary Benson (Atlantic, 2011), prologue.
3  R. H. Benson, Confessions of a Convert (Longmans, Green, 1913), 129.
4  R. H. Benson, The Coward (Hutchinson, 1912), 341–43.

items.title: WOF 546 | Do You Listen to Your Conscience?
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

What does it mean to listen to your conscience, especially in a culture that scoffs at the existence of moral values?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. What does it mean to listen to your conscience, especially in a culture that scoffs at the existence of moral values? Does the concept of conscience still mean anything today? Or is it a relic of what the secular world would have us believe was a naïve and superstitious past—a time of cartoon crickets and buzz-killing angels perched on our shoulders, scolding us into acting against our desires? Was the atheist Sigmund Freud right that conscience is merely the internalized echo of a tyrannical father, seeking to keep our conduct in check? And even if we grant that conscience has some kind of objective existence, how can we account for the fact that people reach radically incompatible moral conclusions while all claiming to follow it? For example, one person says conscience leads them to support abortion; another says conscience requires them to stand against it. Through all of this, how can we say that the conscience is “free” if its primary function is to impose rules? Here to help us untangle these questions, and to make the case that recovering the biblical conception of the conscience is more important than ever, is Bishop Robert Barron.

Topics Covered

00:00 | Introduction
01:24 | Bishop Barron in Nashville: Good News Conference, Dominicans, and Theo Von
02:29 | What is the conscience?
05:21 | Is conscience just a gut feeling?
07:14 | The “angel” and the “devil” on our shoulders
09:57 | Perceiving conscience as an external voice
11:30 | Freud’s concept of the internalized voice of authority
16:04 | Both radically individual and universally shared
